title: Git
description: History editing, recovery, branching, internals and the AOSP repo/Gerrit workflow.

questions.question: What does 'git reset --soft HEAD~1' do?

answers.text: Moves the branch back one commit and keeps the changes staged
Deletes the last commit and all its changes
Creates a new commit that undoes the last one

questions.explanation: --soft keeps index and working tree; --mixed (default) unstages; --hard discards changes.

questions.question: How do you undo a commit that has already been pushed to a shared branch?
questions.explanation: revert adds a new commit and doesn't rewrite shared history.

questions.question: You lost a commit after a bad rebase. What helps to find it again?
questions.explanation: The reflog records where HEAD and branches pointed, typically for 90 days.

questions.question: What does git bisect do?

answers.text: Binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug

questions.explanation: Mark commits good/bad (or use 'git bisect run <script>') until the first bad commit is found.

questions.question: What is the difference between HEAD~2 and HEAD^2?

answers.text: HEAD~2 is the grandparent; HEAD^2 is the second parent of a merge commit
HEAD^2 is the grandparent; HEAD~2 the second parent

questions.explanation: ~ follows first parents; ^n selects the n-th parent.

questions.question: What does 'detached HEAD' mean?

answers.text: HEAD points directly to a commit, not to a branch

questions.explanation: New commits there are only reachable via HEAD/reflog until you create a branch.

questions.question: Which statements about rebase vs. merge are correct?

answers.text: Rebase rewrites commits and gives a linear history
Merge keeps the original commits and adds a merge commit (unless fast-forward)
Rebasing commits that others already use can cause trouble

questions.explanation: Golden rule: don't rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others build on.

questions.question: Why use 'git push --force-with-lease' instead of '--force'?

answers.text: It refuses to overwrite remote commits you haven't seen

questions.explanation: It protects against overwriting a colleague's push made since your last fetch.

questions.question: Which object types does Git store?
questions.explanation: The fourth type is the annotated tag. Git stores snapshots, not diffs (packfiles use deltas internally).

questions.question: You added a file to .gitignore, but Git still tracks it. Why?

answers.text: .gitignore only affects untracked files; use 'git rm --cached <file>'
The .gitignore must be committed first, then it works automatically

questions.explanation: Already tracked files stay tracked until removed from the index.

questions.question: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

answers.text: fetch only downloads; pull fetches and then merges or rebases
pull only downloads; fetch also merges

questions.explanation: 'git pull --rebase' (or pull.rebase=true) rebases local commits on top of the fetched branch.

questions.question: How can you fix an older commit before pushing, keeping history clean?

answers.text: git commit --amend on the older commit directly

questions.explanation: --amend only changes the latest commit; fixup commits are squashed into their target automatically.

questions.question: What does git cherry-pick do?

answers.text: Applies the changes of an existing commit as a new commit on the current branch
Moves a commit to another branch and deletes it from the original
Selects files for the next commit

questions.explanation: Common for backporting fixes between release branches.

questions.question: What does git worktree allow?

answers.text: Several working directories for the same repository, e.g. two branches at once

questions.explanation: Handy for reviewing or building another branch without stashing your work.

questions.question: What does git rerere do when enabled?

answers.text: Remembers conflict resolutions and reuses them when the same conflict appears again

questions.explanation: 'Reuse recorded resolution' helps with repeated rebases of long-lived branches.

questions.question: In AOSP/Gerrit, how do you push a change for review?
questions.explanation: Gerrit creates a change per commit; repo upload wraps this for multi-repo projects.

questions.question: What is the Change-Id footer in Gerrit commits for?

answers.text: It identifies the change across new patch sets (amended commits)
It is the SHA-1 of the commit
It links the commit to a Jira ticket

questions.explanation: A commit-msg hook adds it. Keep it when amending so Gerrit creates a new patch set.

questions.question: Which repo command updates all projects of an AOSP checkout?
questions.explanation: Useful flags: -c (current branch only), -j (parallel jobs), --no-tags.

questions.question: How do you find the commit that added or removed a specific string?
questions.explanation: The 'pickaxe' -S searches for changes in the number of occurrences; -G takes a regex.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git stash pop' and 'git stash apply'?

answers.text: pop applies the stash and removes it; apply keeps it in the stash list
apply removes it; pop keeps it

questions.explanation: If pop hits a conflict, the stash entry is kept.
